en.p: As shown in the figure, quadrilateral $\mathrm{ABCD}$ is inscribed in a circle with $\overline{\mathrm{AB}}:\overline{\mathrm{CD}}=1:3$ and $\overline{\mathrm{BC}}<\overline{\mathrm{AD}}$. Let $\mathrm{P}$ be the point where line $\mathrm{AB}$ meets line $\mathrm{CD}$.

The following is the process of finding the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $\mathrm{BPC}$ when $\overline{\mathrm{PB}}:\overline{\mathrm{PC}}:\overline{\mathrm{BC}}=7:5:\sqrt{14}$ and $\overline{\mathrm{AD}}=4\sqrt{13}$.

box: Let $\angle\mathrm{BPC}=\theta$. Since $\overline{\mathrm{PB}}:\overline{\mathrm{PC}}:\overline{\mathrm{BC}}=7:5:\sqrt{14}$, by the law of cosines in triangle $\mathrm{BPC}$, $\cos\theta=\dfrac{6}{7}$.

By a property of circles, triangles $\mathrm{BPC}$ and $\mathrm{DPA}$ are similar, so $\overline{\mathrm{PB}}:\overline{\mathrm{PC}}=\overline{\mathrm{PD}}:\overline{\mathrm{PA}}$ and $l=\boxed{\ (\text{A})\ }\times k$.
Since the similarity ratio of triangle $\mathrm{BPC}$ to triangle $\mathrm{DPA}$ is $1:\boxed{\ (\text{B})\ }$, $\overline{\mathrm{BC}}=\dfrac{1}{\boxed{\ (\text{B})\ }}\times\overline{\mathrm{AD}}$.
Therefore, if $R$ is the radius of the circumcircle of triangle $\mathrm{BPC}$, then by the law of sines in triangle $\mathrm{BPC}$, $R=\boxed{\ (\text{C})\ }$.
